title_en: Chicago’s City Council Orders Independent Review of Finances as Scrutiny Intensifies
excerpt_en: The post Chicago’s City Council Orders Independent Review of Finances as Scrutiny Intensifies appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Alderperson Pat Dowell, center, chair of the Finance Committee, speaks to reporters following a Chicago City Council meeting on Wednesday. Dowell called for an outside review of the city’s finances. Victor Hilitski/WTTW News The debate over Chicago’s financial struggles — out in the open as never before — took a new turn on Wednesday as the City Council added to the scrutiny.
The City Council voted 45-5 in a special meeting to give a leading alderperson the authority to hire an outside firm to independently review Chicago’s finances.

It’s unclear if an audit would be complete in time for the City Council to consider its findings before the Dec. 29 deadline mandated by state law to pass a 2027 budget, in what likely will be contentious negotiations with Mayor Brandon Johnson. Later in the day came another sign of distress: S&P Global put the city on credit watch with a warning that the budget wrangling is likely to result in a credit downgrade within 90 days.

The intense council debate over the city’s financial future comes in the wake of a package of stories published Monday by WTTW News and ProPublica that examined how a $55 billion debt burden, decades in the making, was hampering efforts to service Chicagoans and how the Johnson administration was turning to more borrowing to plug holes, such as large police settlements.

Alderperson Pat Dowell had called for the outside review after former Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch abruptly resigned Friday over what she described as a political environment that forced her to downplay certain facts about the city’s financial situation. Gabrysch argued that her integrity would be compromised if she stayed on.

Just as Gabrysch had once been a trusted part of Johnson’s team, Dowell was once thought to be a mayoral ally. Johnson tapped Dowell, who endorsed him during the 2023 mayoral election, to lead the City Council’s Finance Committee soon after he took office.

But since then Dowell has proven to be a thorn in the mayor’s side, refusing last year to support his proposal to impose a $25 per month per employee tax on most firms that have more than 125 employees and hike the city’s personal property lease tax. (Johnson continues to push for that idea.)

The ordinance gives Dowell the authority to spend whatever is necessary “to determine whether any material or intentional misstatements of the city’s financial condition to investors, the City Council and the public have been made in any public document, presentation, offering or financial reporting within the prior three years.”
The firm, or firms, hired to conduct the review will have access to all city documents and records, and all city officials must cooperate with the probe, according to the ordinance.

“We must ensure that our math is correct,” Dowell said, vowing to act quickly. “The discrepancies over the past few weeks have been particularly disturbing to me. As my mother used to say, where there’s smoke, there’s fire.”
Johnson said he welcomed the review and will not veto the ordinance.

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson presides over a special City Council meeting on Wednesday. Victor Hilitski/WTTW News Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said he wasn’t certain an audit was warranted while acknowledging its importance in another way. He noted that the audit vote coupled with the inability of the council and the mayor to agree on a budget plan already may have done damage with credit rating agencies.
“The way cities make their budgets matter,” Marlowe said. “It matters that for the third year in a row that there are disagreements over basic facts.”
In short, Marlowe said, “Investors don’t like uncertainty, and this is creating a lot of uncertainty.”
Alderperson Matt Martin said Wednesday that the analysis by ProPublica and WTTW was “sobering.” He is questioning some of Johnson’s borrowing strategies.

Over the years, Chicago alderpersons have generally acquiesced to mayoral directives on finances. But that has changed under Johnson, in part due to his preference for a head tax but also because of the growing realization that the city’s finances have been undermined by a series of decisions from previous mayors.
Similarly, top administration officials generally choose to leave City Hall either quietly or with words of praise for the current mayor. That’s not how Gabrysch handled her exit.

The statement she released Friday made it clear she had severe doubts about the way Johnson was portraying the city’s debt problem. And she reiterated those concerns in a commentary in the Chicago Tribune over the weekend that also laid out her suggestions for how the city can more responsibly handle its budgeting (for example, “Don’t borrow to pay everyday bills, even if we’ve done so in the past”).
Then, in a brief interview with the Chicago Sun-Times on Monday, she said she supported calls for a financial audit.

“If this makes it easier for residents to see that Chicago actually is in a fairly dire fiscal situation where hard decisions … and shared sacrifices have to be made, that can be helpful,” Gabrysch said. “Shining some light on the city’s finances — whether or not they discover wrongdoing, but rather showing the nuances of how dire some things have become — could be worthwhile.”

Chicago’s credit rating has been plummeting, adding to the cost of borrowing and leaving the city just two or three levels above junk status among leading Wall Street rating agencies. Gabrysch had been hired just three months ago from Fitch Ratings, with an eye toward shoring up the city’s reputation.

title_en: Apec summit live: Xi, Trump and Putin set to hold historic trilateral in China
excerpt_en: Leaders of the US, China and Russia to take part in their first trilateral, with developments on trade, AI and global conflicts closely watched
body_en: Key event There has been both warm welcomes, and muted greetings on the red carpet rolled out at Apec, writes the Guardian’s Japan correspondent, Justin McCurry.
Military bands played, dozens of cheering young men and women waved colourful bouquets, and senior officials offered hugs and handshakes on the tarmac.
But there was one exception: Japan ’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.
Read the full story below on what was behind it all.
Related: China gives Japan PM frosty welcome at Apec amid fanfare for other leaders
Along with the coterie of world leaders at Apec, hundreds of business leaders are also in Shenzhen, with executives from BYD, Baidu, Boeing and Google set to attend.
Elon Musk is also expected to be there, along with Visa CEO Ryan ⁠McInerney, Mastercard CEO Michael Miebach and Deloitte CEO Joe Ucuzoglu.

Despite the high-profile roster of names, Nikkei Asia has reported that the number of prominent US executives appears “relatively light” compared to previous years. One official told the publication that executives had not been provided with clear agendas in advance and many were caught up in scheduling conflicts.

One major name present at the event in South Korea last year, but noticeably absent from this year’s summit, is Jensen Huang, who resigned from Nvidia last week after a scandal over an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.

South China Morning Post reports that the chaos that has engulfed the chipmaker in the last week has played a role in discouraging some US business leaders from attending the summit, as they “worry about being perceived as close to China”.
Zak Dychtwald, the founder of BridgeWorks Global, a China-based consultancy told the paper that “CEOs had spent the last 18 months returning to China with more confidence, and this sets that back”.

'Passengers riding the same ship' Here’s the Guardian’s Rebecca Bailey on Xi Jinping’s speech today, in which she writes that he reiterated themes of openness and innovation emphasised throughout the summit.

“China is an advocate, promoter and forerunner of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation,” he said. He announced China would give US$20 million in funding “to support APEC’s practical cooperation”, and would establish a Apec-focused research centre in Shenzhen.
“Efforts should be made to align various regional economic and trade agreements, boost trade and investment facilitation and digitalisation, and reduce barriers to trade and investment,” he said.

The region should promote connectivity and innovation, he added. Green energy, energy and food security and digital infrastructure were all among areas mentioned for more coordination and collaboration.
Toward the beginning of his speech he had this poetic flourish:
Members of Apec are like passengers riding the same ship. To navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other.
Trump on AI President Trump has shared some of of his thoughts on AI saying that Apec opposes regulation that would “stifle” the industry.
“We won’t allow that to happen,” he said.
Commenting on concerns about AI, the US president said:
It’s almost completely good, but it’s got some bad elements and we have to be very careful” in managing the bad.
'The fanfare, the pageantry' Trump said his meeting on Thursday with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin was already a “win” before it took place, Reuters news reports.

title_en: Australia may have ‘one foot in recession’ as unemployment surges to five-year high
excerpt_en: Jobless rate rises from 4.7% to 4.9% in October, Bureau of Statistics figures reveal
body_en: Australia may already have “one foot in recession” after unemployment surged to 4.9% in October, from 4.7%, in a shock increase that will add to rising worries that this year’s five interest rate hikes have pushed the economy past a tipping point.
New figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed the number of employed people dropped by 43,500 in the month, confounding forecasts for jobs growth and a steady jobless rate.
Financial markets moved quickly to price out any chance of a sixth Reserve Bank rate increase, and were factoring in a rate cut by September of next year, according to National Australia Bank.

After starting the year at 4%, unemployment has now lifted to its highest level in five years to approach pre-Covid levels. In a further sign of deteriorating conditions, the number of employed Australians has dropped in three of the past four months.

Interactive David Bassanese, the chief economist at Betashares, said there were lingering questions over the seasonal movements in the labour force data that could be giving a falsely weak picture of the jobs market.
“If these employment declines prove to be real, however, they’re the type of weakness that could well mean we’ve seen the last interest rate hike,” Bassanese said.
“Indeed, consecutive large employment declines might suggest the economy already has one foot in recession.”

The shock figures validate warnings from the three dissenting RBA board members, who voted against the Melbourne Cup day rate hike and warned of a “materially sharper downturn” in the economy as households struggled to deal with this year’s substantial lift in borrowing costs.
Related: General Pants Co enters voluntary administration, putting hundreds of jobs at risk
Full-time employment dropped by 2,900 in October, the ABS data showed, and part-time employment by a steeper 40,600 people.

Amid rising concerns about the impact of AI on entry-level roles and the recent string of layoffs in the retail sector, the ABS also flagged another rise in the youth unemployment rate to 11.3% in October, from 11.1% the month before.
Sean Crick, the head of labour statistics at the ABS, said “this is the highest it’s been since October 2021”.
“In the post-Covid period (from May 2022 onwards), the youth unemployment rate has averaged 9.2%,” Crick said.
Sunny Nguyen, the head of Australia economics at Moody’s Analytics, said “the Aussie labour market has unmistakenly turned”.
Nguyen said the latest data “all but closes the door” on any chance of a pre-Christmas rate hike.
“For the RBA, this lands on a board already split over whether policy has gone far enough,” he said.
“The bank only lifted its unemployment forecast earlier this month to peak above 5% by the end of 2028; the labour market is within sight of that level two years early.”

Taylor Nugent, a senior economist at National Australia Bank, said there was a risk the jobless rate could begin to accelerate as rising unemployment hit spending and, in turn, forced employers to further tighten their belts.
“We had been expecting peak unemployment to peak at around 5.5% by the end of next year. This [latest data] does suggest that it’s playing out a bit faster than we had been expecting.”

title_en: Russian national charged with spying on Silicon Valley tech and defense firm
excerpt_en: Igor D’iu is alleged to have unlawfully entered US and reportedly gathered intel about Palantir and its employees
body_en: The US Department of Justice has accused a Russian national of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company in an alleged effort to gather intelligence for Russia.

On Wednesday, the justice department announced that Igor D’iu had been indicted on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the attorney general, interstate stalking and fraud involving identification documents.

According to officials, D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully this summer after being recruited by co-conspirators through Telegram. His alleged mission was to “carry out clandestine assignments targeting employees of a large technology and defense company with an office in Palo Alto, California”, the justice department said, without identifying the company or the alleged co-conspirators.
Related: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years in US prison over Trump murder plot
Bloomberg reported that the company in question was Palantir Technologies, citing an unnamed source familiar with the matter. The firm has a large office in Palo Alto.
The department added that D’iu had reportedly received instructions, equipment and financial support from the co-conspirators, who told him that his work was for “the Motherland”.
They also allegedly instructed him to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine.
The Russian embassy was contacted for comment.

In June, D’iu allegedly traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City, where his co-conspirators connected him with an individual who helped him cross the US-Mexico border. After entering the US, he was allegedly instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software to “facilitate his assignments”.

D’iu’s co-conspirators also allegedly directed him to visit a cafe near the company’s Palo Alto office, identify employees and photograph their laptop screens as they worked. They further instructed him to “position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity”, the justice department said.

The alleged surveillance gradually expanded, with D’iu allegedly instructed to monitor employees and their residences. The justice department said he reportedly conducted online searches for multiple employees’ home addresses, including that of a senior executive.

In early September, D’iu allegedly followed a female employee in a silver Lexus SUV for nearly 30 miles (48km) as she drove from the company’s Palo Alto office toward San Francisco. According to the justice department, the employee repeatedly attempted to evade him, at one point driving into a grocery store parking lot.

Officials said D’iu “allegedly aggressively continued following her, including through U-turns and illegal left turns, and ran a red light to remain behind her vehicle”. The employee eventually called 911 and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco police department’s Mission station.

D’iu allegedly abandoned the pursuit after the employee contacted a police officer. The justice department added that investigators had also obtained evidence indicating he had followed other employees on previous occasions.

After Palo Alto police contacted D’iu about the alleged stalking incident, he reportedly changed vehicles and obtained a new phone number. His co-conspirators then allegedly instructed him to travel to Reno, Nevada, before he returned to the Bay Area to continue his assignments, the justice department said.

The justice department also accused D’iu of obtaining fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity. Investigators reportedly intercepted two international packages containing concealed ID documents, including a fake California ID card and an altered US passport. Officials said the passport was authentic and had originally been issued to another individual in the US before being modified to display D’iu’s photograph and assumed identity.

Investigators also discovered a social security card bearing the name “Hugo Landry Johns”. During an FBI search of D’iu’s East Palo Alto residence in October, investigators recovered approximately $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, two Russian passports, wireless networking equipment and additional fraudulent ID documents.

They also found a notebook containing 10 handwritten addresses, several of which belonged to the residences of company employees. The notebook also included detailed profiles of at least three employees, documenting their family members’ names, educational and employment histories, and an “assessment of their strengths and weaknesses”.

In response to the indictment, M Scott Proctor, acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, said: “The Americans who build our defense technology help keep this country safe by arming our warfighters with the tools and weapons they need to prevail against our adversaries and enemies.

“As alleged, D’iu entered our country illegally at the direction of foreign handlers to surveil, follow and gather information about some of those who work in this vital industry. Such conduct, if proven, is a flagrant violation of US sovereignty and an unacceptable attempt at intimidation,” he added.

title_en: Florence Pugh speaks out against ‘disturbing’ cosmetic surgery speculation
excerpt_en: Actor criticises ‘stressful’ online conjecture in lengthy statement after photos of her at the Governors awards went viral, denying she had ever been on Ozempic or had surgery
body_en: Florence Pugh has said she is “disturbed” by a flurry of “stressful” online speculation about her appearance after images of her at the Governors awards this week went viral.

The 30-year-old actor wrote a lengthy statement to her 11 million Instagram followers on Wednesday in which she denied speculation that she had undergone cosmetic surgery or used weight-loss injections.
“I find it so stressful waking up and have thousands of people talking about you and your body in ways that you can’t even comprehend,” she wrote.

“I woke up the other morning and quite a lot of you were discussing my face and body in such a disturbing way. I learnt online that I had been on Ozempic? I learnt that I’d had upper bleph[aroplasty]? Lower bleph? Filler? Face lipo[suction]? Buccal fat remover? Chin surgery? Nose surgery?!”
Related: East of Eden review – Florence Pugh in soapy Steinbeck adaptation is brilliant, compelling TV
The Dune, Thunderbolts and Oppenheimer actor continued: “Yes, I’m disturbed. For women who now think that I’m someone I’m not. For having my body dissected and pointed at again.

“I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow. I was subjected to fat shaming in the business from the moment I started and I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I’m not changing that now just because you’ve all said so.”
Pugh, who is known for speaking out about beauty standards and scrutiny of women’s bodies in Hollywood, insisted she had not undergone cosmetic procedures.
“I have never been on Ozempic, I have NEVER done any face surgery. And don’t EVER say that I didn’t make my own nose,” she wrote. “I’ve always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!”
Pugh said she had made a series of lifestyle changes since turning 30, including “chang[ing] my relationship with alcohol and to be able to do at least one pull-up in the gym.”

“It’s funny to see you all use reference images from times where I was really mentally unhappy and abusing my body, and put it next to the image from the Governors awards the other night where I am happy and truly respecting my body,” she wrote.
“For the first time in my ENTIRE career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily.”
Pugh said she had worked hard to improve her physical and mental wellbeing, adding: “I’m looking after myself, and that’s literally it.”

Reflecting on the criticism she has faced throughout her career, she said: “I’ve always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that.
“But now this…? I’m asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives.”

Pugh also claimed she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs.
“I was fucking horrified,” she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.
Pugh concluded by urging followers to reflect on their attitudes towards physical appearance and the pressures of changing beauty standards.
“But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people’s physical appearance,” she wrote. “I’m not angry at you, I’m angry at the situation that’s being projected onto us.
“It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye.”

In 2022, Pugh hit back at “vulgar” social media users who criticised her body after she posted photographs of herself wearing a sheer dress designed by Valentino’s creative director Pierpaolo Piccioli to one of the brand’s shows.
“What happened to you to be so content on being so loudly upset by the size of my boobs and body?” Pugh wrote at the time.

title_en: Beijing has three priorities at the Shenzhen summit – a China expert explains
excerpt_en: The Apec summit offers a window into what China hopes to achieve on the international stage as well as the world it perceives itself in.
body_en: China is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit for the third time in the past 25 years. The gathering in Shenzhen will see the leaders of the US, China and Russia sit down together for a formal three-way meeting for the first time in history.

But what does China want from the summit? I see it as having three main priorities. First is to consolidate its position as one of the world’s most important diplomatic hubs. Second is to set out its vision for a new global order.

And third is to take advantage of favourable geopolitical conditions, primarily brought about by US setbacks in Iran and Russia’s quagmire in Ukraine, to adjust the terms of its engagement with Washington and Moscow.

1. A diplomatic hub Hosting national leaders and other high-level officials has become a key feature of Chinese diplomacy in recent years. President Xi Jinping has welcomed over 25 world leaders to China so far in 2026. These include Canada’s Mark Carney, Germany’s Friedrich Merz, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez and the UK’s former prime minister, Keir Starmer.

Beijing’s push to become a key diplomatic convener is a notable break from earlier forms of Chinese diplomacy. In the 2010s, the assertive and confrontational approach of Chinese officials on the international stage was widely known as “wolf warrior” diplomacy.

The name is derived from a series of patriotic Chinese action films, also called Wolf Warrior. In this period, Chinese officials used social media to share controversial political memes and spar with foreign politicians and critical journalists, drawing condemnation in diplomatic circles.

This belligerent approach was retired in the early 2020s. Notable wolf warriors such as China’s former foreign affairs minister Qin Gang and ministry spokesman Zhao Lijian were reassigned or removed from their posts.
China’s hosting of the latest Apec summit is in line with Beijing’s new diplomatic strategy, suggesting it has acknowledged the limitations of the wolf warrior approach.

2. Reshaping the global order As well as showcasing China’s shifting approach to diplomacy, hosting major international events such as the Apec summit is a central part of Beijing’s wider ambitions to reshape the global order – most notably as a venue to gain greater legitimacy for its vision.

This vision was summarised in a 45-page white paper released by China’s state council in June. The paper signalled the Chinese government’s desire to evolve from being a participant of the existing international system to the architect of a new global order where China and the global south play a greater role.

The same message was repeated in the run-up to the Shenzhen summit. In a speech in late October, China’s foreign affairs minister Wang Yi declared that “the rise of the global south is the most momentous shift since the second world war”.

He framed China’s hosting of multilateral events such as Apec as a vehicle to give developing countries a greater voice on the international stage. It is this vision that China seeks to convey to the wider world through the Shenzhen summit.

3. Great-power engagement The timing of the Shenzhen summit works in China’s favour. With the US and Russia currently bogged down in costly military conflicts in Iran and Ukraine respectively, and Trump reeling from a punishing electoral defeat, it is Xi who holds the strongest geopolitical hand.

When Trump, Putin and Xi sit down together in Shenzhen on November 19, China may be in a position to push harder on the terms of its engagement with Washington and Moscow. A primary goal for China is to stabilise the global economy, which has been disrupted by the war in Iran.

However, many commentators remain sceptical that the three-way meeting will deliver any concrete outcomes. The US and China recently extended their fragile trade truce, delaying the expiry date until January 2027. Preventing relations from deteriorating is thus probably in the interests of both countries.

And on various other issues, the three leaders are entering the meeting with vastly different ambitions. Trump is focused primarily on agreeing a three-way nuclear arms control agreement. But China has historically refused to discuss any limitations on its nuclear arsenal while its stockpile of warheads remains smaller than the US and Russia’s.

On the other hand, Russia has pushed to make Ukraine a central part of the talks. It is aiming to build support for a settlement to the war on terms favourable to Moscow. However, China has sought to keep Ukraine off the agenda entirely, fearing political backlash and deeper economic countermeasures from the EU should it back such a settlement.
Regardless of this, the 2026 Apec summit offers a window into what China hopes to achieve on the international stage as well as the world it perceives itself to be in.

Tom Harper does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title_en: They Were Just Admitted to the Bar. Now They’re Federal Prosecutors. Meet Trump’s New DOJ.
excerpt_en: The post They Were Just Admitted to the Bar. Now They’re Federal Prosecutors. Meet Trump’s New DOJ. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Michelle Urra for ProPublica In early October, a recent law school graduate shared a post on LinkedIn that would have been unheard of before the second Trump administration.

After passing the bar exam, 29-year-old Preston Bigley wrote, “With this milestone complete, I will begin serving as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Criminal Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.”

It was a remarkable achievement, considering Bigley had graduated from Texas A&M’s law school in May and had been hired by the Justice Department in August to be, as his resume notes, an “incoming” assistant U.S. attorney. That unusual title was followed by an unusual caveat: “pending bar admission.” Once officially licensed to practice the law, he updated his profile to show he had become a bona fide federal criminal prosecutor.

Bigley is one of a growing cohort of inexperienced attorneys, many of them fresh out of law school, who are being fast-tracked to fill the shoes of seasoned career prosecutors who fled or were purged from the DOJ in President Donald Trump’s second term. That brain drain, amounting to thousands of years of experience, comes as prosecutions of fraud and drugs have fallen in key districts to make way for Trump’s immigration agenda, ProPublica found.

Across the country, ProPublica identified more than 50 new assistant U.S. attorneys with less than three years of experience who traditionally wouldn’t have been considered for such vital positions, legal experts said. Some were hired with the intent to anoint them as prosecutors — once they pass the bar exam, public disclosures show.

That figure is likely a fraction of the actual total, as a comprehensive analysis is impossible because DOJ staff identities are redacted in government personnel data. But of those ProPublica identified through bar membership records and social media, about 20 passed the bar within the last year. At least seven were in the same May graduating class as Bigley, from a range of schools.

“The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of law school — it’s an astounding break with past practice,” said Juliet Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S. attorney. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and bring with them experience beyond just law school.”

To understand how Trump transformed the DOJ, ProPublica examined federal court data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social media accounts. We also interviewed more than two dozen former assistant U.S. attorneys.

More than half of those who left the Justice Department in Trump’s first 18 months boasted nine-plus years of legal experience. Those who left had spent, on average, more than 13 years working for the government, the analysis shows. Those more experienced attorneys were the ones most likely to take on complex cases, such as money laundering, organized crime and drug trafficking, legal experts say and court dockets show.

ProPublica shared its analysis and detailed questions with the DOJ; the department did not respond. Previously, the DOJ said it “remains committed to investigating and prosecuting all types of crime.”

Under Trump’s Second Administration, Newly Hired Assistant U.S. Attorneys Have Less Experience Than Those Who Departed Note: This analysis of federal pay codes does not include experience ranges for supervisors. We also exclude some special assistant U.S. attorneys for whom we cannot infer experience or supervisory status. Pratheek Rebala/ProPublica The DOJ has long hired recent graduates through its Honors Program, which places graduates into rigorous training through the main office in Washington, but experts say the program was small and not meant to replace prosecutors.

Before Trump’s second term, the DOJ typically would not hire new prosecutors unless they had a minimum of three to five years of legal experience, former officials and law professors said. That standard is gone. Earlier this year, Bloomberg Law reported, the DOJ waived a policy requiring at least one year of experience.

While private law firms routinely hire promising graduates before they pass the bar exam, typically to begin their training, the DOJ’s hiring of new grads is a striking departure from its once-rigorous hiring process, said University of Michigan law professor Barbara McQuade, a former U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan.

“The people who I hired came to us as partners in law firms,” said McQuade, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. “These were superstars who had been very successful at large law firms or in state court prosecutors’ offices.”
Trump’s creation of a less experienced DOJ will have longstanding consequences, McQuade said.

“It means that some very serious crimes will go unpunished,” she said. “It takes experienced prosecutors at the federal level to bring down corporate fraud, transnational gangs and corrupt public officials.”

While experts expressed concern, some of those benefiting from the law school-to-federal prosecutor pathway have voiced excitement on LinkedIn. “I look forward to beginning my DOJ career by serving the Del Rio Division,” wrote Jacquelyn Kilcommons, who graduated from Pace University’s law school in May. “Upon receiving my bar exam results, I will transition into an Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA) position.”

As he announced his new role in the district of Washington, D.C., newly graduated assistant U.S. attorney Ellis O’Donnell wrote, “In the past few months I have had the honor to graduate from Vanderbilt University Law School and to sit for and pass the Wisconsin Bar Exam.” None of the recent law school graduates responded to requests for comment.

title_en: A good-news story to rouse us oldies | Brief letters
excerpt_en: Brief letters: Alzheimer’s medication | The price of fish | Brussels sprout tops | Outage v failure | People and places | Orienteering in Ikea
body_en: At last, a welcome good-news story ( Pill that mimics Viagra can slow Alzheimer’s progression, study suggests, 18 November). Now we seniors will be able to have sex and remember we have done so. John Lovelock Bristol

• Has anybody thought of using smoked salmon units to measure the cost of living? Our local deli sells half-sides of smoked salmon for Christmas. Twenty years ago, they were £25, this year they are £55! Rod Moreton Ampleforth, North Yorkshire

• One nutritious and delicious option that Rachel Dixon didn’t mention ( The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings, 17 November) is brussels sprout tops. Not as widely available as they should be, these are the equal of any green cabbage. Neil Angrave London

• John Dwyer asks ( Letters, 16 November), and I can answer. An outage is the effect; failure is the cause. Quite important to distinguish the two, especially if you are trying to fix a problem. Dick Quibell London

• My husband, setting out on a bike ride from Oxford, asked: “Should I visit the Chilterns, the Astons or the Barringtons?” It took me a while to realise that these were places, not people ( Letters, 15 November). Susan Hutchinson Oxford

title_en: World ‘held hostage by oil mafia’, says Panama minister at Cop 31
excerpt_en: Key issues unresolved as summit enters final days, with 30 countries signed up to forge fossil fuel treaty separate to UN process
body_en: The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister has warned, as key issues remain unresolved in the final days of the UN Cop31 climate summit.

“We are in love with our kidnappers,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, at a press conference to announce 30 countries were now signed up to forge a new fossil fuel treaty, separate to the UN process. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”

Expressing the frustration shared by scores of developing countries and thousands of civil society activists at these talks, he added: “They torture us for our own good, they destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love. And we are so stupid that we fall for it.”

Countries have only two official days of negotiation left at Cop31 to resolve key issues, such as whether the conference should recognise the need to “transition away from fossil fuels” and how to address the “overshoot” of global temperatures beyond the 1.5C of heating targeted in the Paris agreement.

The Australian presidency of the talks and the Turkish hosts convened a “divan” meeting of ministers on Wednesday evening. Named for the Ottoman empire’s term for a council or assembly, the aim of the meeting was to make progress on a revised draft of a possible outcome and find compromises on sticking points. Significant dividing lines remain on issues such as climate finance, how to ensure a “just transition” to clean economy jobs for workers in fossil fuels and helping poor countries adapt to the impacts of extreme weather.

The first draft of a “cover decision”, issued on Monday, contained 144 separate items, including several – such as the “transition away from fossil fuels” – that some of the nearly 200 countries at the fortnight-long talks find contentious. There are concerns that the Australian approach of including “everything” in the draft text may result in longer negotiations. A new draft is expected on Thursday morning.

A breakthrough from the “divan” meeting was not expected, but negotiators told the Guardian that countries were working together on compromises. Campaigners feared that the outcome would be feeble, however.

Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, accused rich countries of offering “crumbs” to a fund for the developing world to adapt to extreme weather. Only $50m has been pledged so far, compared with $135m last year.

“Rich countries are offering crumbs to the adaptation fund, while blocking the negotiations that should provide the money countries need,” he said. “Listening to ministers praise the adaptation fund before giving next to nothing, you have to wonder how they expect it to do the work they say is so important.”

There was anger, too, over the “just transition mechanism”, which is intended to help developing countries ensure workers in high-carbon industries can be retrained or helped, while they grow nascent green industries. “We’re seeing massive steps backwards on adaptation finance and just transition, relative to previous Cops,” said Brandon Wu, the director of policy and campaigns at the ActionAid USA charity. “In both cases, the blocking is being led by the EU.”

Irene Vélez Torres, the former Colombian minister who convened talks in Santa Marta in April on the phaseout of fossil fuels, said she was worried about a target to generate 35% of final energy from electricity by 2035, which is thought to have the explicit support of at least 60 countries, and the tacit support of more, including China. Like many campaigners, she would like to see provisions that ensure the electricity comes from renewable sources.

“I’m very scared that [the target] is not going to be explicit about clean green energy, because it may imply that they are going to lock us in future dependencies on gas and coal power. If we don’t explicitly declare that the electricity is going to be powered by green and clean energy, we may make a mistake,” she said.

Frustrated with the slow speed of the UN talks, some countries have been using Cop31 to further their own alternatives. Colombia has changed governments since Vélez convened talks on a “transition away from fossil fuels” in April, but the Santa Marta process carries on, with Tuvalu hosting the next meeting.

The Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, with 30 members, at whose event Navarro was speaking, is another attempt to create a “coalition of the willing” to phase fossil fuels out, as is the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance.

Ethiopia, which will host the Cop32 meeting next year, is leading a group of countries that want to go further than phasing fossil fuels out. The “group of negative emitters” aim to absorb more carbon than they produce, by using carbon capture technology or growing trees and restoring natural “carbon sinks”, such as wetlands and peatlands.

“Slashing emissions is essential but no longer enough,” said Ani Dasgupta, the president of the World Resources Institute thinktank. “We must also actively pull carbon out of the atmosphere, to bring temperatures back down.”

Samuel Addis Alemayehu, the Ethiopian ambassador, called for financial help for poor countries to follow through with their plans. “Ethiopia is expanding nature-based solutions [such as tree-planting] and calls for scaled-up support, adequate finance and access to technologies that reduce emissions,” he said.

title_en: Xi-Trump-Putin summit: when great powers want to call all the shots, what does it mean for everyone else?
excerpt_en: In such a world, power determines not only outcomes, but who gets invited into the room when outcomes are being discussed.
body_en: Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump are meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.
The meeting is no doubt unusual – a very rare opportunity for the leaders of the world’s three major powers to exchange views directly on major global issues.

It’s drawn comparisons to the Yalta conference of 1945, when US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian leader Joseph Stalin met to divide the world into spheres of influence after the second world war.

But this is no Yalta 2.0. Nor is the Shenzhen summit an isolated episode. In May this year, Xi hosted back-to-back visits by Trump and Putin to Beijing. Trump reciprocated by hosting Xi in Washington in September, and met with Putin in Alaska last year.

Taken together, these developments signal a broader shift away from the post-Cold War emphasis on global institutions and multilateral consultations toward a more personalised form of great power management.
This is likely the new normal: a world in which China, Russia and the US act as an informal steering committee for global affairs, with Europe and other middle powers increasingly on the sidelines.

Who’s invited into the room While China, Russia and the US remain strategic competitors, they increasingly share an understanding of how international politics should be conducted: less through institutions and coalitions, and more through direct engagement among a small number of major powers.

This is by no means a formal alliance – not even between China and Russia – or a coordinated redesign of the international system. Rather, it reflects a common instinct toward great-power management of international affairs.

All three favour a world in which major powers enjoy special rights and a privileged voice in shaping outcomes, negotiating major questions directly while limiting others’ involvement. Whether discussing war, security issues or economic stability, the major powers increasingly appear willing to bypass institutional channels in favour of high-level, direct diplomacy.

For instance, Russia and the US just concluded a third round of peace talks this year in Abu Dhabi towards ending the Ukraine war. While Ukraine was part of the discussions, European negotiators were not.
In such a world, power determines not only outcomes, but who gets invited into the room when outcomes are being discussed.
Europe increasingly on the sidelines The most obvious casualty of this trend is Europe.

During the Abu Dhabi talks last week, the Russian delegation made clear it wanted a new security framework for Europe modelled after the spheres of influence that existed during the Cold War. Trump has also flagged this as a possibility, saying the US was working on a big deal to end the war that would include “all of Europe”.

After the talks, US special envoy Jared Kushner said Washington wanted Europe to be part of the process. He added, however, that finding someone who could credibly speak for Europe might be harder than persuading Russia to include them – a provocative statement.
These comments have set off alarm bells in Europe and reinforced a growing perception that Europe is increasingly fragmented and marginalised as an actor in global politics.

More significant, however, is that Xi ultimately agreed to join the Shenzhen trilateral summit. Having seen Europe sidelined from the Abu Dhabi talks, his decision to meet with Trump and Putin risked legitimising that exclusion, even if Ukraine is not on the agenda.

That looks awkward for China, given Xi’s repeated emphasis on multipolarity and criticism of Cold War-style politics dominated by a few major powers. Beijing has also previously stressed that Europe should be “at the table” for Ukraine discussions.

And yet Xi has agreed to meet with Trump and Putin. Moreover, China’s Foreign Ministry described the summit as having “groundbreaking significance”. The three leaders would “exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations,” it said.
This suggests Beijing accepts a model of diplomacy centred on major powers, to the exclusion of others.
And this creates an uncomfortable reality for Europe.
Europe remains one of the world’s largest economic and technological centres, but it struggles to translate that weight into a unified strategic voice that carries weight on the global stage.
The symbolism of the Shenzhen meeting is telling. Three leaders will be discussing issues that affect Europe’s future. And again, Europe itself will not be present.

title_en: Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era
excerpt_en: Pattinson could be seen as the safe choice but his back catalogue belongs to an actor who is capable of surprise.
body_en: James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

Next up, Pierce Brosnan incarnated a glamorous post-cold-war masculinity, with his lingering sexism teased out by Samantha Bond’s witty Moneypenny and the disruptive casting of Judi Dench as M, the head of MI6. And in the 2000s, Daniel Craig’s Bond was a physically tough but emotionally vulnerable character. His wounded body and scarred mind linked emotional detachment to childhood trauma.

Pattinson’s career Pattinson’s acting credentials make him one of the most established actors to take on the role. Since the Twilight saga (2008-2012), he has grown to be among the more versatile actors of his generation, with a penchant for challenging, often downright strange roles.

From the psychological intensity of Good Time (2017) to Robert Eggers’s claustrophobic gothic The Lighthouse (2018), the characters he has played are anything but straightforward leading men. Even when turning to action, his Batman (2022) was unexpectedly brooding and introspective.
There is certainly scope with his casting to extend the darker vision of Bond first introduced by Dalton and subsequently developed by Craig.

Visually, too, Pattinson seems almost a composite of previous Bonds. Declared the world’s most handsome man in 2020, Pattinson has the chiselled good looks of Brosnan. Although he might not have Connery’s physique, the intense training he underwent for Batman suggests that he could manage the demanding physical aspects of the role. This, however, may be more challenging, given that Pattinson, at 40, is already ten years older than former producer Barbara Broccoli had anticipated the next Bond would be in 2024.

Pattinson’s Bond As a white Englishman whose image is associated with an upper-middle-class, heterosexual masculinity, Pattinson might seem a safe, even predictable, choice for Bond. And yet, he is not unfamiliar with the challenge of portraying unconventional masculinity.

In Little Ashes (2008), he explored the young Salvador Dalí’s intimate relationship with the poet Federico García Lorca. Much like Craig, he has shown himself willing to explore queer desire and the instability of masculine identity.
I think what Craig’s era could have done more with is humour, and Pattinson might well bring a fresh comic sensibility to the next incarnation of Bond.

Beneath his often brooding intensity lies a nuanced comic performer. Humour has allowed Pattinson to question conventional masculinity in some of his roles. In Damsel (2018), he challenged the traditional western hero by playing an inept cowboy whose masculine confidence far exceeded his capabilities. Elsewhere, his darkly camp rendition of Louis the Dauphin in The King (2019), the tragi-comic The Drama (2026) and the self-aware short Fear & Shame (2017) all seemingly serve to undermine male vanity.

Perhaps Pattinson’s history of darkly strange and funny characters will create space for this new Bond to, playfully or otherwise, explore our current preoccupations with toxic masculinity, sexual consent and male vulnerability.

Fleming thought of his secret agent as an “unobtrusive … neutral figure – an anonymous blunt instrument”. Screenwriter Steven Knight now faces the challenge of using Bond as a blank canvas to highlight the clash between the character’s traditional roots and modern culture.
Read more: I write James Bond novels – here’s why Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight will bring a crackling new intensity to 007
In particular, the new Bond would benefit from a more diverse supporting cast whose backgrounds are woven naturally into the story, reflecting his global audience without feeling forced.

I’m thinking female characters not defined by their relationships with Bond, villains who call out Bond’s elitism, queer characters that could complicate his seemingly straight world. Bond girls and villains will play a crucial role in delivering these (or failing to do so). But it will be Pattinson and his choices for this iconic character at the centre of it all, deciding whether the franchise will sink or swim.

Monica Germanà does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title_en: I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life.
excerpt_en: The post I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: I read once that photographers have ongoing conversations with one another across space and time. When Evelyn leaned back on the examination table at her doctor appointment, I instantly thought of W. Eugene Smith’s 1948 Life Magazine photo essay, “Country Doctor.” Smith’s photograph of the doctor taking a smoke break and this photograph of Evelyn have, strangely, so much in common. About eight years ago, I was assigned to photograph the sentencing of Travis and Sarah Mitchell, a couple with deep roots in an insular faith-healing sect outside of Portland, Oregon.

The Mitchells, as members of the Followers of Christ, adhere to a doctrine that forbids medical care. Instead, followers rely on healing through faith. So when Sarah Mitchell gave birth prematurely to twins in 2017 — and both gasped for breath in their first hours — the couple didn’t rush them to an emergency room. Instead, they turned to prayer.

One twin, Ginnifer, lived for four hours, each one a struggle. The family eventually sought medical care for her surviving twin sister, Evelyn, but only after the county’s deputy medical examiner arrived at the location of the home birth and learned, though not right away, of Evelyn’s existence. Even then, he had to seek help from police, who arrived at the Oregon City home and told reluctant family members to take the struggling infant to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.

The Mitchells pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide in the death of their infant daughter, Ginnifer, and to criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for her surviving twin, Evelyn. The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to ProPublica and The Oregonian’s recent requests to be interviewed.)

Today, my memory of the sentencing is more montage than detail. But I remember the crowded gallery, the couple in black-and-white-striped prison clothing, and their prison sentence of more than six years. Evelyn, who within days of her birth had been placed in the custody of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, another couple in the Followers of Christ, wasn’t present. She remained in the couple’s permanent care.
The Mitchells went off to prison, and I went on with my life.

Such is the grinding rhythm of the daily news cycle. So often I see people on their worst day — and then never again. Stories don’t really end, of course, but my role as a photojournalist is limited. I’m an observer rather than a participant, seeing mostly slivers of the human experience that offer only a window into the whole. It’s rare that I get to see what happens next.

Never would I have dreamed that the surviving baby in this case, Evelyn, would be someone I’d later come to know and care about through my work. But that’s precisely what happened eight years after that courtroom scene played out, when I began documenting the lives of Evelyn and her parents, the Phillipses. (In a legal filing in an ongoing case relating to Evelyn’s custody, the Mitchells criticized the Phillipses for allowing her to participate in our coverage.) The resulting story, a collaboration between ProPublica and The Oregonian, is one of several recently published about faith healing and the Followers of Christ church. It intimately explores the Phillipses’ journey out of the sect and illustrates how changes in Oregon state law — in contrast to neighboring Idaho, where the Followers have a handful of churches — have led to a reduction in child deaths.

To spend time around 9-year-old Evelyn is to behold a luminous, magnetic force of nature. It’s impossible to imagine this same girl as a premature baby so small that the only items that fit her were doll clothes purchased from the supermarket toy aisle.

For months, as I documented Evelyn’s life — from her baptism to her home life to doctors’ appointments — my journalism colleagues worked on their own pieces of our project. Teresa Mahoney, video editor at The Oregonian, produced a video introduction to the story that included a sequence of footage recorded by body cameras worn by police officers who stood outside Evelyn’s grandparents’ house that night, at first nudging, then ordering, Evelyn’s family to get her to the hospital. Each time I viewed it, as I watched the officers politely letting time slip away, I’d need to regulate my own breathing as I imagined Evelyn on the other side of that door, struggling to breathe herself.

I hope that reporter Noelle Crombie’s words, Teresa’s video and my photographs allow readers to see not only the journey of the couple who are raising Evelyn as their own but also the surviving — indeed, thriving — twin I came to know. That Evelyn is alive at all is, depending on your worldview, a miracle.
My work is all about observing and capturing moments, about freezing time. Here, I was witnessing the unfolding of time. I got to see what happened next.

Evelyn’s baptism was a highly anticipated day and meaningful for all involved. The stakes were high for me because the immersion lasted only a few seconds. I had one chance to get it right. Jennifer Phillips is a steadfast presence in Evelyn’s life. This moment of her curling Evelyn’s hair in preparation for the baptism reminded me of daguerreotypes from the 1800s. In some, mothers who wanted photographs of their babies had to hold them behind velvet drapes so as not to be visible in the portraits. I thought of the nature of emotional labor and how much of it is unseen. Evelyn was getting a kick out of giving Marshall a pounding back massage. We were all at McDonald’s — her favorite restaurant — having her birthday meal. Marshall Phillips and Evelyn attended a father-daughter dance at a high school a few towns away. Evelyn had a list of dances she and Marshall practiced. I had recently lost my father and was carrying grief. But seeing Marshall’s love for Evelyn was beautiful and healing. In person, Evelyn sparkles. When she saw herself in a mirror with her face painted, her delight was electric. The night before Evelyn’s ninth birthday party, the family decorated the room where the event would take place. I know firsthand how much parenting involves endless tasks and routines. Mixed into the chaos are moments of pure joy. Yearly pediatric check-ups are an ordinary aspect of childhood, and for Evelyn it’s no different. Knowing her history, however, gives these moments an undeniable poignance. A check on her heart rate becomes a reminder of the miracle of her very existence. Before bed, Marshall reads a chapter book to Evelyn that combines the concept of evolution with lessons from the Bible. Evelyn was excited I was there and sprinkled in knock-knock jokes between the biblical passages. After that, the family prays together. Although Evelyn didn’t know the other kids at the father-daughter dance, she seemed to make friends easily. Here, she formed a conga line with a group of girls.
